planting.note: Establish from plugs or sod (not seed) once soil is reliably above 70F; a female, vegetatively propagated buffalograss cultivar grown alongside Prairie, 609, and Legacy as a turf-type selection bred for lawn use rather than rangeland or forage.

directions: Stampede is a vegetatively propagated buffalograss cultivar, established only from plugs or sod since it does not come true from seed. Like other vegetative buffalograss selections it forms a dense, fine-bladed sod once knitted together, needing very little supplemental water once established and going dormant to a straw-brown color over winter before greening up again in late spring. It is grown as a lower-input alternative to seeded buffalograss cultivars where uniform coverage matters more than up-front cost, filling in more evenly across a planting site than broadcast seed. Mow occasionally at 3 to 5 inches for a tidier lawn, or leave unmowed for a naturalized, low-water planting, and avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization or overwatering, both of which invite weed competition into buffalograss's naturally thin, open canopy.

planting.note: Establish from plugs or sod (not seed) once soil is reliably above 70F; a female vegetative buffalograss line developed through the University of Nebraska-Lincoln turfgrass breeding program, noted for strong performance in the northern and transition zones of the buffalograss range.

directions: '378' is a vegetative, female buffalograss selection from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln's turfgrass breeding program, propagated only from plugs or sod since it does not produce viable seed suitable for lawn establishment. It has shown particularly strong turf performance toward the northern and transition-zone edge of buffalograss's adapted range compared to older vegetative types, holding density and color well under the shorter growing seasons found there. As with other buffalograss selections it needs very little supplemental irrigation once established, going dormant and straw-colored over winter and greening up again in late spring. Mow at 3 to 5 inches occasionally, or leave unmowed as a low, drought-tolerant lawn, and avoid high-nitrogen fertility programs that favor weeds over buffalograss's naturally open sod.

planting.note: Establish from plugs or sod (not seed) once soil is reliably above 70F; recommended by University of Missouri Extension alongside Bonniebrae, Prairie, and 609 for lawns in the transition zone.

directions: Mobuff is a vegetatively propagated, female buffalograss cultivar included among the vegetative selections recommended by University of Missouri Extension for lawns in the transition zone, established only from plugs or sod rather than seed. Like other vegetative buffalograss types it produces a more visually uniform stand than seeded cultivars once fully knitted in, since every plant is a genetic clone rather than a variable seedling. It shares buffalograss's hallmark low water and fertility needs, holding up through summer drought with little supplemental irrigation and going dormant to a tan-brown color in winter before regreening in late spring. Mow occasionally at 3 to 5 inches, or leave unmowed for a low, naturalized lawn, and avoid overwatering or heavy fertilization, which encourage weed encroachment into buffalograss's open, low-growing canopy.

planting.note: Establish from plugs or sod (not seed) once soil is reliably above 70F; listed among commercially available vegetative turf-type selections alongside Mobuff, Prairie, and 609.

directions: Bonniebrae is a vegetatively propagated, female buffalograss cultivar established only from plugs or sod, part of the same class of clonal turf-type buffalograss selections as Mobuff, Prairie, and 609. Because it is planted as living plant material rather than seed, it fills in as a genetically uniform stand, avoiding the patchiness that can come from variable seedling populations in seeded buffalograss lawns. It carries buffalograss's characteristic drought tolerance, needing minimal irrigation once rooted in, and follows the same seasonal pattern of summer green growth and straw-brown winter dormancy. Mow at 3 to 5 inches occasionally for a groomed look, or leave unmowed as a low-water native lawn, and keep fertility and irrigation modest to avoid inviting weed pressure into its naturally open canopy.

common_name: Scaldis Hard Fescue (Classic Low-Input No-Mow Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in lean, well-drained soil; a longstanding hard fescue cultivar included in university low-input and no-mow fine fescue evaluations.

directions: Scaldis is a longstanding hard fescue cultivar that has appeared for decades in university no-mow and low-input fine fescue trials, including California evaluations comparing mowed and unmowed performance. Left unmowed it forms a low, tufted meadow-like turf that has rated consistently acceptable for color and quality in extension trials, though under regular mowing it can thin out over time and become more susceptible to weed encroachment than some newer hard fescue releases. Like other hard fescues it tolerates poor, infertile, and acidic soils and needs minimal fertilizer or irrigation, making it a fit for dry shade plantings and naturalized lawn areas rather than high-traffic turf. Sow in early fall into a lean, well-drained seedbed, keep it moist through germination, and taper off water once established.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Nordic Hard Fescue (NTEP-Tested Drought-Tolerant Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in lean, well-drained soil; a hard fescue cultivar from Zajac Performance Seeds evaluated in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program fineleaf fescue trials for summer density and disease resistance.

directions: Nordic is a hard fescue cultivar from Zajac Performance Seeds that has been carried through National Turfgrass Evaluation Program fineleaf fescue trials, where it has been noted for excellent summer turf density, good drought tolerance, and solid overall disease resistance including summer patch. As a bunch-type hard fescue it forms a fine-textured, upright stand well suited to dry shade, infertile soils, and low-input lawn or roadside seeding rather than high-traffic turf, and it depends on overseeding rather than lateral spread to repair worn or bare areas. It needs little supplemental fertilizer or water once established, tolerating the kind of lean, acidic soil that stresses Kentucky bluegrass and bermudagrass. Sow in early fall into a well-drained seedbed, keep consistently moist through germination, and mow high and infrequently, or not at all.

common_name: Defiant Hard Fescue (Consistent Regional-Trial Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in lean, well-drained soil; regional Mid-Atlantic trials have found Defiant and Minotaur to be among the most consistently performing hard fescue cultivars across varied climate sites.

directions: Defiant is a hard fescue cultivar that has performed consistently across multiple climatic trial sites in Mid-Atlantic regional turfgrass evaluations, alongside fellow hard fescue Minotaur, with good overall disease resistance among its notable strengths. Like other hard fescues it grows as a fine-textured, upright bunchgrass suited to dry shade, low-fertility soils, and low-input or unmowed lawn plantings rather than high-wear turf, relying on overseeding rather than lateral spread to fill in damaged areas. It requires little supplemental water or fertilizer once established and tolerates acidic, infertile soils better than Kentucky bluegrass or perennial ryegrass. Sow into a lean, well-drained seedbed in early fall, keep moist through germination, and mow high and infrequently, or leave unmowed.

common_name: Minotaur Hard Fescue (Regional-Trial Top-Performing Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in lean, well-drained soil; evaluated in the National Turfgrass Evaluation Program fineleaf fescue test and paired with Defiant as one of the most consistent hard fescue cultivars in Mid-Atlantic regional trials.

directions: Minotaur is a hard fescue cultivar evaluated in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program fineleaf fescue trials, where it has shown excellent summer density and good drought tolerance, and it was identified alongside Defiant as one of the most consistently performing hard fescue cultivars across varied Mid-Atlantic climate sites. As a bunch-type hard fescue it forms a fine, upright stand best suited to dry shade, poor soils, and low-mow or unmowed lawn areas rather than high-traffic turf, filling in worn spots only by overseeding rather than lateral spread. It needs little supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established, handling acidic and infertile soils far better than Kentucky bluegrass or bermudagrass. Sow in early fall into a lean, well-drained seedbed, keep evenly moist until germination, and mow high and infrequently.

common_name: Culombra Chewings Fescue (NTEP Drought-Recovery Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil; a Chewings fescue cultivar carried through National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials for its color retention and recovery following extended drought.

directions: Culombra is a Chewings fescue cultivar evaluated in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials, where it has been noted for retaining color well through extended dry periods and recovering quickly once moisture returns, a valuable trait for low-input lawns that see minimal supplemental irrigation. Its narrow, upright leaf blades and bunch-type growth habit give it a fine, dense texture that blends readily with other fine fescues in low-maintenance and shade seed mixes. It tolerates dry shade and infertile, acidic soils considerably better than Kentucky bluegrass, and it is commonly grown in no-mow or low-mow lawn plantings across the cooler regions of the country. Sow in early fall, keep the seedbed consistently moist until germination, and expect a period of summer dormancy under prolonged heat rather than year-round green color.

common_name: SR 5100 Chewings Fescue (Seed Research of Oregon Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil; a Chewings fescue cultivar from Seed Research of Oregon that is a certified Oregon seed crop commonly blended into low-maintenance eco-lawn seed mixes.

directions: SR 5100 is a Chewings fescue cultivar developed and marketed by Seed Research of Oregon and listed among certified fine fescue varieties in the Oregon certified seed program. It is frequently included as one of several fine fescues in low-maintenance eco-lawn style seed blends, valued for fine leaf texture and among the strongest shade and drought tolerance of the cool-season turf species, which lets it get by with far less mowing than ryegrass, tall fescue, or Kentucky bluegrass. As a bunch-type Chewings fescue it depends on overseeding rather than lateral spread to fill bare patches, and it performs best in lean, well-drained soil rather than heavy, wet ground. Sow in early fall, keep consistently moist through germination, and mow high and infrequently, or leave unmowed.

common_name: SR 5130 Chewings Fescue (Rutgers-Oregon Cooperative Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil; developed through cooperative research between Rutgers University and Seed Research of Oregon, adaptable to both sun and shade.

directions: SR 5130 is a Chewings fescue cultivar that came out of cooperative breeding work between Rutgers University and Seed Research of Oregon, prized for being unusually adaptable to both full sun and shade as well as to high- or low-maintenance management regimes. It is known for strong color retention, fine leaf texture, and good disease resistance, holding its own in mixed company with other regional fine fescue comparisons. As a bunch-type fescue it forms a dense, fine turf well suited to low-input lawns and shaded areas where bluegrass and ryegrass struggle, though it relies on overseeding rather than spreading growth to repair worn patches. Sow in early fall into a well-drained bed, keep moist through germination, and mow high and infrequently to keep the stand dense and shade-competitive.
sources: Rutgers University Center for Turfgrass Science

common_name: Shadow III Chewings Fescue (High-Endophyte Disease-Resistant Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil; third-generation successor in the Shadow line of Chewings fescue, selected for improved turf quality, disease resistance, and high natural endophyte content.

directions: Shadow III is the third generation in the Shadow line of Chewings fescue cultivars, bred for improved turf quality and disease resistance over its predecessors along with high levels of naturally occurring endophyte, which helps deter some surface-feeding insects without chemical inputs. Like other Chewings fescues it forms a fine, dense, bunch-type turf well suited to shaded lawns and low-input seed mixes, tolerating dry, infertile, and acidic soils far better than Kentucky bluegrass or perennial ryegrass. It depends on overseeding rather than lateral spread to fill in bare or worn patches, so it performs best in lawns with light to moderate traffic rather than heavy-wear areas. Sow in early fall into a well-drained bed, keep consistently moist through germination, and mow at a relaxed height to preserve density and shade tolerance.

common_name: Pernille Creeping Red Fescue (Widely Grown European-Bred Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow at 4-5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall, or early spring in short-season climates; one of the more widely grown strong creeping red fescue cultivars used in low-input lawn and shade seed mixes.

directions: Pernille is a strong creeping red fescue cultivar that spreads slowly by short rhizomes, giving it a somewhat greater ability to knit together a self-repairing sod and fill small bare patches than the purely bunch-type hard and Chewings fescues. It shares the fine fescue group's tolerance for dry shade, low fertility, and acidic soils, needing far less water and fertilizer than Kentucky bluegrass or tall fescue to hold acceptable turf quality. It is commonly blended into low-maintenance and shade-tolerant lawn seed mixes rather than seeded alone, and it tends to develop brown leaf tips if mowed too closely or too infrequently, so it performs best at a relaxed mowing height or left unmowed in naturalized plantings. Sow in early fall, or in early spring in the shortest-season climates, keep the seedbed evenly moist through germination.

common_name: Grande II Tall Fescue (Rhizomatous Self-Repairing Turf-Type Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall, or in early spring; a rhizomatous tall fescue (RTF) cultivar bred to produce enough underground rhizome growth to self-repair bare or worn turf areas, unlike most bunch-type tall fescues.

directions: Grande II belongs to the rhizomatous tall fescue (RTF) category of turf-type tall fescue cultivars, bred to produce meaningful underground rhizome growth so the turf can spread laterally and repair bare or damaged patches on its own, a genuine advantage over the purely bunch-type habit of most tall fescue. It keeps the deep taproot system and drought tolerance characteristic of tall fescue as a species, giving it a long green season and good performance under low-input, infrequent-irrigation management, while tolerating fairly tall mowing heights without losing its upright, visually dense growth habit. It is well suited to home lawns and landscape plantings, and its self-repair capability makes it useful for areas that see occasional heavy wear, such as play areas, without requiring regular overseeding. Seed into a firm, fertile bed in late summer or early fall so roots establish before winter, or seed again in early spring if needed, and mow at 3 to 4 inches for best density.

common_name: Cochise III Tall Fescue (High-Endophyte Sports-Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall, or in early spring; a turf-type tall fescue from Ampac Seed Company bred with a high natural endophyte level for improved persistence and stress tolerance on high-traffic turf.

directions: Cochise III is a turf-type tall fescue cultivar from Ampac Seed Company bred with an unusually high natural endophyte level, reported around 88 percent, that improves persistence and stress tolerance compared with lower-endophyte tall fescue cultivars. That combination of traits has made it a popular choice for high-traffic sports fields and other demanding turf applications where wear tolerance and recovery matter as much as appearance. Like other tall fescues it keeps a deep, drought-tolerant root system and a bunch-type growth habit, so it depends on overseeding rather than lateral spread to fill bare or worn patches, though its endophyte-driven persistence reduces how often that overseeding is needed. Seed into a firm, fertile bed in late summer or early fall, or again in early spring, and mow at 3 to 4 inches, avoiding scalping that stresses the crown.

common_name: DeltaShade St. Augustine Grass (Shade-Bred Proprietary Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently above 70F; a proprietary St. Augustine cultivar released in 2005 by Environmental Turf and bred primarily for improved shade tolerance.

directions: DeltaShade is a proprietary St. Augustine grass cultivar released in 2005 by Environmental Turf and bred with a focus on improved shade tolerance, though university trials rate it as somewhat behind the more shade-specialized dwarf cultivars such as Palmetto and Seville. It has a lighter green color than many other St. Augustine cultivars and is reported to have good cold tolerance, though that trait has not been independently verified through university research the way it has for cultivars like Raleigh. Install sod or plugs in spring through midsummer and keep consistently moist through establishment, then mow at 3.5 to 4 inches, since St. Augustine cannot recover well from scalping that removes its green leaf tissue. It spreads by above-ground stolons like other St. Augustine cultivars, filling in bare patches over a season under good conditions, and should be watched for chinch bugs and gray leaf spot common to the species in hot, humid climates.
